How a Rainbow Begins

A rainbow forms when sunlight interacts with tiny water droplets suspended in the air. Although sunlight looks white, it contains many wavelengths of visible light, corresponding to different colors. When sunlight enters a raindrop, it slows slightly and bends because light travels differently through air and water. This bending is called refraction. Different wavelengths bend by slightly different amounts, so the white light begins separating into its component colors.

What Happens Inside the Droplet

  1. Sunlight enters the droplet and refracts.
  2. The separated light reflects from the droplet’s inner surface.
  3. The light exits the droplet and refracts again, increasing the separation between colors.

Millions of droplets perform this process simultaneously. Only droplets positioned at suitable angles send particular colors toward an observer’s eyes. For the primary rainbow, the strongest light arrives roughly 40–42 degrees from the point opposite the Sun. Because each color leaves droplets at a slightly different angle, red appears on the outer edge while violet appears on the inner edge.

A rainbow therefore is not a physical object located at one fixed place. Its apparent position depends on the observer, the Sun, and the illuminated droplets. Another person nearby technically sees light coming from a different collection of droplets.
